results.title: Stopping Rules and Dose Limiting Toxicity (DLT) Criteria in Phase 1 Trials – Clinical Research Made Simple
results.content: # Stopping Rules and Dose Limiting Toxicity (DLT) Criteria in Phase 1 Trials. Stopping Rules and Dose Limiting Toxicity (DLT) Criteria in Phase 1 Trials. # Stopping Rules and Dose Limiting Toxicity (DLT). One of the most critical aspects of early-phase trial design is the implementation of **stopping rules and Dose Limiting Toxicity (DLT) criteria**. These safety mechanisms ensure that trials are halted or adjusted when adverse events (AEs) suggest that further exposure at a given dose is unethical or potentially harmful. ## What Are Dose Limiting Toxicities (DLTs)? They help determine the *maximum tolerated dose (MTD)* and inform decisions about escalation, de-escalation, or stopping. Any event that qualifies as a DLT within this window may affect cohort progression or trial continuation. ## What Are Stopping Rules? **Stopping rules** are prespecified safety conditions that, if triggered, lead to the temporary or permanent halt of:. * Dose escalation to the next cohort. ## Types of Stopping Rules. * If ≥2 out of 6 participants at a dose level experience DLTs, escalation is halted. Pharmacokinetic (PK)-Driven Stopping Rules. ## Designing DLT and Stopping Rules in Protocols. Stopping rules and DLT definitions must be clearly described in the protocol. In many early-phase trials, a Data Monitoring Committee (DMC) or **Safety Review Committee (SRC)** is established. * Reviews all AE and DLT data after each cohort. ## Real-World Example: How DLT Criteria Stopped a Trial. As per the stopping rule of ≥2 DLTs in 6 subjects, escalation was paused. ## Adaptive Escalation with Stopping Rules. Modern dose escalation designs (like CRM or BOIN) incorporate stopping rules algorithmically:. * **FDA**: Expects stopping rules to be pre-specified in the protocol under IND. * **EMA**: Requires stopping rules and DLT definitions per “Guideline on strategies to identify and mitigate risks for FIH and early clinical trials.”. * Define both drug-related and unrelated stopping rules (e.g., device failure, protocol deviation). * Conduct simulations to validate stopping rule robustness before trial start. Stopping rules and DLT criteria serve as critical safeguards in Phase 1 clinical trials.

results.title: Patient Safety Management in Early Phase Clinical Trials
results.content: It provides valuable insights into the safety profile of the investigational product and helps sponsors to proactively identify and manage potential safety risks, optimize dose selection, establish robust safety monitoring plans, manage adverse events and implement risk mitigation strategies during early phase clinical trials. By analyzing the pre-clinical safety data, researchers can anticipate and monitor specific adverse events during the clinical trial. For example, based on pre-clinical safety data of a new anti-cancer drug, a comprehensive adverse event management plan was developed for the clinical trial. **Practical Tip:** Incorporate the dose-related adverse events observed in pre-clinical studies into the safety monitoring plan for the clinical trial. By analyzing the pre-clinical data, researchers were able to develop appropriate monitoring protocols and safety measures to detect and manage potential adverse events in human subjects. Integrating pre-clinical data into the clinical trial design and safety monitoring processes enhances the understanding of the investigational product’s safety profile and aids in early detection and management of adverse events.

results.title: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures: OWASP Top 10
results.content: THE ACUNETIX BLOG Web Security Zone # Security logging and monitoring failures: OWASP Top 10 Security logging and monitoring failures are one of the most commonly overlooked risks in application security. ## What are security logging and monitoring failures? Security logging and monitoring failures occur when critical security events are not properly recorded, monitored, or reviewed. * Logs missing key details (e.g., timestamps, IP addresses, user actions) * Lack of real-time monitoring to detect threats as they happen * Logs stored insecurely or not retained long enough * Systems failing to alert teams to genuinely suspicious behavior * Inconsistent logging practices across applications or environments * Insufficient protections against log tampering These gaps reduce visibility into application activity and increase the likelihood that attacks will go unnoticed. ## What are the risks of improper security logging and monitoring? ## Security logging and monitoring failure example In July 2024, a single content update from cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike cascaded into a global crisis, causing over 8.5 million systems to crash worldwide. What transformed this incident from a mere technical mishap into a profound security logging and monitoring failure was its multilayered blindness. This case study powerfully demonstrates how even sophisticated, well-intentioned automated security processes can become devastating points of failure when logging and monitoring mechanisms aren’t designed to detect errors within the security tools themselves. ## Improving security logging and monitoring Proactive measures can help teams gain clarity and control over their environments: * Log key security events like logins, privilege changes, and access to sensitive data. Security teams, developers, and IT operations must collaborate to define what gets logged, how it’s monitored, and who can access those records. ## How DAST can also help with security logging and monitoring Dynamic application security testing (DAST) tools simulate real-world attack scenarios in production-like environments. This approach helps validate whether: * Logging systems capture relevant attack data * Detection workflows are tuned to real-world behavior rather than theoretical vulnerabilities DAST can reveal blind spots and streamline the tuning of detection systems to focus on practical threats—especially helpful for teams with limited time or resources. ## Final thoughts on preventing security logging and monitoring failures Security logging and monitoring should not be an afterthought—they are essential components of any effective security strategy.

results.title: Escalation | Remote Patient Monitoring
results.content: Health services using RPM must develop escalation pathways and contingency strategies for effective patient monitoring and clinician response. These should include decision-making processes for patients who require escalation of care, and formal documented arrangements between the service and receiving hospital. When developing escalation pathways for RPM, services should collaborate with both clinicians and patients to understand their insights into managing escalations effectively. * authorise and support the RPM clinician, patient or family member or carer to escalate care until they are satisfied that an effective response has been provided. Clinicians should be aware of local escalation procedures and the clinical emergency response system (CERS) protocol for instructions on making a call to escalate care. If a service aligns its monitoring to the Clinical Excellence Commission Between the Flags (BTF) deteriorating patient safety net system and the standardised calling criteria in the accompanying NSW Health observation charts, clinicians must follow the prescribed steps outlined in the relevant charts when:. * As part of the escalation procedure for clinical deterioration, some patients will be identified as needing a clinical review. A clinical review in this circumstance is a review of a deteriorating patient undertaken by the clinical team responsible for the patient’s care as per the local CERS protocol. * Clinical review must be initiated following the local escalation procedures and CERS, aligning with NSW Health Policy Directive Recognition and management of patients who are deteriorating (PD2020\_18). * Clinical review is essential to manage deteriorating patients and must be conducted by experienced clinical staff. * The decision to initiate a clinical review must be made in consultation with a clinical supervisor and documented in the patient’s health record. * Local services should determine the review timeframe; the clinician most appropriate to conduct the review; and other related responses based on the RPM model of care and the clinical risks associated with care delivery. * As part of the escalation procedure for clinical deterioration, some patients will need a rapid response. * A rapid response must be initiated according to the local escalation procedures and  CERS, aligning with NSW Health Policy Directive Recognition and management of patients who are deteriorating (PD2020\_18). ## Clinical escalation pathway.
